theory.overview: I/O systems handle communication between programs and the outside world. Event loops enable efficient handling of many concurrent I/O operations without blocking. Understanding I/O models (blocking, non-blocking, asynchronous) is crucial for writing scalable servers and responsive applications.

sections.title: Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O
sections.content: Blocking I/O waits for the operation to complete before returning. Non-blocking I/O returns immediately, indicating whether the operation completed or would block.

sections.title: Event Loops
sections.content: An event loop continuously checks for I/O events and invokes callbacks when events occur. This enables a single thread to handle thousands of concurrent connections efficiently.

examples.explanation: Single thread handles many connections via callbacks

sections.title: select vs epoll vs kqueue
sections.content: Different OS APIs for monitoring multiple file descriptors. select() has O(n) overhead. epoll (Linux) and kqueue (BSD) use efficient data structures for O(1) operations.

steps.title: File Descriptors
steps.content: Everything is a file in Unix. File descriptors are integers representing open files, sockets, or pipes. Operations like read(), write(), close() work on all types.

steps.title: The select() Loop
steps.content: Build a set of file descriptors to monitor. select() blocks until any is ready. Iterate through descriptors to find which ones need attention and process them.

steps.title: epoll & Scalability
steps.content: epoll (Linux) scales better than select() for many connections. It uses a kernel-side data structure and notifies only ready descriptors, avoiding O(n) scans.

practiceProblems.title: Event Loop Order
practiceProblems.description: In an event loop, if fd1 and fd2 are both ready, which is processed first?
practiceProblems.solution: Depends on implementation. Typically the one with lower fd number or the one that was registered first. Order shouldn't matter for correctness.

practiceProblems.title: C10K Problem
practiceProblems.description: Why can't thread-per-connection handle 10,000 concurrent connections?
practiceProblems.solution: Thread stacks consume memory (~8MB each = 80GB). Context switching overhead becomes significant. Thread creation/destruction is expensive.
